content: The second edition of the Guidance for National Tuberculosis Programmes on the Management of Tuberculosis in Children was developed to provide updated recommendations for the diagnosis, treatment, prevention, and control of tuberculosis (TB) in children. This document builds upon the first edition, published in 2006, which led to the revision or creation of national guidelines for managing childhood TB in many high-burden countries. However, new evidence and recommendations necessitated an update to the original guidance. The second edition aims to assist national and regional TB control programs in revising their existing guidelines and standards for managing TB, particularly in children. It includes evidence-based recommendations to improve the management of children with TB and those living in households affected by TB. The guidance also emphasizes the importance of adapting these recommendations to local circumstances. Since 2006, there has been increased attention to the unique challenges of TB in children and its recognition as a significant global public health issue. While children with TB may not contribute significantly to community transmission, the disease remains a critical cause of morbidity and mortality among children and mothers. Following the publication of the 2006 guidance, many countries developed national policies and strategies to address childhood TB. However, practical implementation of these strategies has often been limited. The current challenge is to bridge the gap between policy and practice by scaling up childhood TB activities in endemic countries. This second edition introduces several important changes and additions compared to the first edition. It includes separate chapters on topics previously covered only in annexes, such as the management of TB/HIV co-infection in children and drug-resistant TB in children. It also introduces new topics, such as the importance of integrated care and the management of TB in adolescents, recognizing their vulnerability and the lack of specific focus on this group in existing guidelines. The preparation of this second edition adhered to the World Health Organization's (WHO) process for developing evidence-based guidelines. It incorporates current WHO recommendations from previously published documents on TB and HIV management. Any earlier recommendations that have been revised in terms of detail, strength, or quality of evidence are highlighted in this document. The guidance underscores the urgent need for more epidemiological data on childhood TB in high-burden countries and further research into the immunological and pathological differences between children and adults with TB. This research is essential for developing and evaluating better tools for prevention, diagnosis, and treatment. Despite these gaps, there are already many actionable steps that can be taken to reduce the burden of TB in children. The development of this guidance involved a Guidelines Development Group (referred to as the Panel), which provided expert advice throughout the process. The Panel included experts from various institutions who contributed their time and expertise to discussions and activities related to the update. An External Review Group also provided feedback on the draft document. All members of the Panel and the External Review Group completed declarations of interest, which were reviewed to ensure no conflicts of interest. The WHO Global TB Programme acknowledges the contributions of the Panel members, technical advisors, and other individuals who supported the preparation of this document. The revision process, including the Panel meeting, was funded by the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) under the TB CARE I Collaborative Agreement. The contents of the guidance do not necessarily reflect the views of USAID or the United States Government. The Writing Committee, led by Dr. Stephen Graham, Dr. Malgosia Grzemska, Dr. Suzanne Hill, Ms. Tara Kedia, and Ms. Nicole Wong, finalized the document after review by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee. The guidance represents a consensus effort to address the specific challenges of childhood TB and to provide practical recommendations for improving its management globally.
